senses.d: To die; to perish; hence, to wither; to fade.
To become quelled; to become cast down; to sink under trial or apprehension of danger; to lose the spirit and power of resistance; to lose heart; to give way; to shrink; to cower.
q: The atheist power shall quail, and confess his fears. I. Taylor. Stouter hearts than a woman's have quailed in this terrible winter.

Quail.syn: to cower; flinch; shrink; quake; tremble; blench; succumb; yield.
Quail.etym: [AS. cwelan to die, perish; akin to cwalu violent death, D. kwaal pain, G. qual torment, OHG. quelan to suffer torment, Lith. gelti to hurt, gela pain. Cf. Quell.]

senses.d: To cause to fail in spirit or power; to quell; to crush; to subdue.
To curdle; to coagulate, as milk.

Quail.etym: [OF. coaillier, F. cailler, from L. coagulare. See Coagulate.]

senses.d: Any gallinaceous bird belonging to Coturnix and several allied genera of the Old World, especially the common European quail (C. communis), the rain quail (C. Coromandelica) of India, the stubble quail (C. pectoralis), and the Australian swamp quail (Synoicus australis).

Any one of several American partridges belonging to Colinus, Callipepla, and allied genera, especially the bobwhite (called Virginia quail, and Maryland quail), and the California quail (Calipepla Californica).
Any one of numerous species of Turnix and allied genera, native of the Old World, as the Australian painted quail (Turnix varius). See Turnix.
A prostitute; — so called because the quail was thought to be a very amorous bird.

Quail.etym: [OF. quaille, F. caille, LL. quaquila, qualia, qualea, of Dutch or German origin; cf. D. kwakkel, kwartel, OHG. wahtala, G. wachtel.]

senses.d: To be agitated with quick, short motions continually repeated; to shake with fear, cold, etc.; to shudder; to tremble.
q: She stood quaking like the partridge on which the hawk is ready to seize.

senses.d: To shake, vibrate, or quiver, either from not being solid, as soft, wet land, or from violent convulsion of any kind; as, the earth quakes; the mountains quake.

Quake.etym: [AS. cwacian; cf. G. quackeln. Cf. Quagmire.]

senses.d: To cause to quake.

Quake.etym: [Cf. AS. cweccan to move, shake. See Quake, v. t.]

senses.d: A tremulous agitation; a quick vibratory movement; a shudder; a quivering.

The attribute of being so much, and not more or less; the property of being measurable, or capable of increase and decrease, multiplication and division; greatness; and more concretely, that which answers the question “How much?”; measure in regard to bulk or amount; determinate or comparative dimensions; measure; amount; bulk; extent; size.
That which can be increased, diminished, or measured; especially (Math.), anything to which mathematical processes are applicable.

A determinate or estimated amount; a sum or bulk; a certain portion or part; sometimes, a considerable amount; a large portion, bulk, or sum; as, a medicine taken in quantities, that is, in large quantities.
q: The quantity of extensive and curious information which he had picked up during many months of desultory, but not unprofitable, study.

Quantity.etym: [F. quantite, L. quantitas, fr. quantus bow great, how much, akin to quam bow, E. how, who. See Who.]

senses.d: A quarry.
An arrow for a crossbow; — so named because it commonly had a square head.
q: To shoot with arrows and quarrel.
Two arblasts, . . . with windlaces and quarrels.

senses.d: Any small square or quadrangular member
A glazier's diamond.
A four-sided cutting tool or chisel having a diamond-shaped end.

Quarrel.etym: [OE. quarel, OF. quarrel, F. carreau, LL. quadrellus, from L. quadrus square. See Quadrate, and cf. Quadrel, Quarry an arrow, Carrel.]

senses.d: A breach of concord, amity, or obligation; a falling out; a difference; a disagreement; an antagonism in opinion, feeling, or conduct; esp., an angry dispute, contest, or strife; a brawl; an altercation; as, he had a quarrel with his father about expenses.
q: I will bring a sword upon you that shall avenge the quarrel of my covenant.
On open seas their quarrels they debate.

senses.d: Ground of objection, dislike, difference, or hostility; cause of dispute or contest; occasion of altercation.
q: Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him.
No man hath any quarrel to me.
He thought he had a good quarrel to attack him.

senses.d: Earnest desire or longing.

Quarrel.syn: Brawl; broil; squabble; affray; feud; tumult; contest; dispute; altercation; contention; wrangle.
Quarrel.etym: [OE. querele, OF. querele, F. querelle, fr. L. querela, querella, a complaint, fr. queri to complain. See Querulous.]

senses.d: To violate concord or agreement; to have a difference; to fall out; to be or become antagonistic.
q: Our people quarrel with obedience.
But some defect in her Did quarrel with the noblest grace she owed.

senses.d: To dispute angrily, or violently; to wrangle; to scold; to altercate; to contend; to fight.
q: Beasts called sociable quarrel in hunger and lust.

senses.d: To find fault; to cavil; as, to quarrel with one's lot.
q: I will not quarrel with a slight mistake.

senses.d: To quarrel with.
To compel by a quarrel; as, to quarrel a man out of his estate or rights.
One who quarrels or wrangles; one who is quarrelsome.
Same as 1st Quarrel.

Quarry.etym: [OE. quarre, OF. quarré square, F. carré, from L. quadratus square, quadrate, quadratum a square. See Quadrate, and cf. Quarrel an arrow.]

senses.d: Quadrate; square.
A part of the entrails of the beast taken, given to the hounds.
The object of the chase; the animal hunted for; game; especially, the game hunted with hawks.
q: The wily quarry shunned the shock.

Quarry.etym: [OE. querre, OF. cuiriée, F. curée, fr. cuir hide, leather, fr. L. corium; the quarry given to the dogs being wrapped in the akin of the beast. See Cuirass.]

senses.d: To secure prey; to prey, as a vulture or harpy.
A place, cavern, or pit where stone is taken from the rock or ledge, or dug from the earth, for building or other purposes; a stone pit. See 5th Mine (a).

Quarry.etym: [OE. quarrere, OF. quariere, F. carrière, LL. quadraria a quarry, whence squared (quadrati) stones are dug, fr. quadratus square. See Quadrate.]

senses.d: To dig or take from a quarry; as, to quarry marble.
The fourth part; a quarter; hence, a region of the earth.
q: Camber did possess the western quart.

Quart.etym: [F. quart, n. masc., fr. L. quartus the fourth, akin to quattuor four. See Four, and cf. 2d Carte, Quarto.]

senses.d: A measure of capacity, both in dry and in liquid measure; the fourth part of a gallon; the eighth part of a peck; two pints.
A vessel or measure containing a quart.

Quart.etym: [F. quarte, n. fem., fr. quart fourth. See Quart a quarter.]

senses.d: In cards, four successive cards of the same suit. Cf. Tierce, 4.
Same as 2d Carte.
One of four equal parts into which anything is divided, or is regarded as divided; a fourth part or portion; as, a quarter of a dollar, of a pound, of a yard, of an hour, etc.
q: Scouts each coast light-armed scour, Each quarter, to descry the distant foe.

senses.d: A division of a town, city, or county; a particular district; a locality; as, the Latin quarter in Paris.
A small upright timber post, used in partitions; — in the United States more commonly called stud.
The fourth part of the distance from one point of the compass to another, being the fourth part of 11° 15′, that is, about 2° 49′; — called also quarter point.
Proper station; specific place; assigned position; special location.
q: Swift to their several quarters hasted then The cumbrous elements.

senses.d: A station at which officers and men are posted in battle; — usually in the plural.
Place of lodging or temporary residence; shelter; entertainment; — usually in the plural.
q: The banter turned as to what quarters each would find.

senses.d: A station or encampment occupied by troops; a place of lodging for soldiers or officers; as, winter quarters.
Treatment shown by an enemy; mercy; especially, the act of sparing the life a conquered enemy; a refraining from pushing one's advantage to extremes.
q: He magnified his own clemency, now they were at his mercy, to offer them quarter for their lives.
Cocks and lambs . . . at the mercy of cats and wolves . . . must never expect better quarter.

senses.d: Friendship; amity; concord.
q: In quarter, and in terms like bride and groom.
I knew two that were competitors for the secretary's place, . . . and yet kept good quarter between themselves.

Quarter.etym: [F. quartier, L. quartarius a fourth part, fr. quartus the fourth. See Quart.]

senses.d: To divide into four equal parts.
To divide; to separate into parts or regions.
q: Then sailors quartered heaven.

senses.d: To furnish with shelter or entertainment; to supply with the means of living for a time; especially, to furnish shelter to; as, to quarter soldiers.
q: They mean this night in Sardis to be quartered.

senses.d: To furnish as a portion; to allot.
q: This isle . . . He quarters to his blue-haired deities.

senses.d: To arrange (different coats of arms) upon one escutcheon, as when a man inherits from both father and mother the right to bear arms.
To lodge; to have a temporary residence.
To drive a carriage so as to prevent the wheels from going into the ruts, or so that a rut shall be between the wheels.
q: Every creature that met us would rely on us for quartering.

senses.d: The number four.
A set of four parts, things, or person; four things taken collectively; a group of four words, phrases, circumstances, facts, or the like.
q: Delivered him to four quaternions of soldiers.
Ye elements, the eldest birth Of Nature's womb, that in quaternion run.
The triads and quaternions with which he loaded his sentences.

senses.d: A word of four syllables; a quadrisyllable.
The quotient of two vectors, or of two directed right lines in space, considered as depending on four geometrical elements, and as expressible by an algebraic symbol of quadrinomial form.

Quaternion.etym: [L. quaternio, fr. quaterni four each. See Quaternary.]

senses.d: To divide into quaternions, files, or companies.
The wife of a king.
A woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom; a female monarch; as, Elizabeth, queen of England; Mary, queen of Scots.
q: In faith, and by the heaven's quene.

senses.d: A woman eminent in power or attractions; the highest of her kind; as, a queen in society; — also used figuratively of cities, countries, etc.
The fertile, or fully developed, female of social bees, ants, and termites.
The most powerful, and except the king the most important, piece in a set of chessmen.
A playing card bearing the picture of a queen; as, the queen of spades.

Queen.etym: [OE. quen, quene, queen, quean, AS. cwēn wife, queen, woman; akin to OS. quān wife, woman, Icel. kvān wife, queen, Goth. qēns. √221. See Quean.]

senses.d: To act the part of a queen.
To make a queen (or other piece, at the player's discretion) of by moving it to the eighth row; as, to queen a pawn.

To extinguish; to overwhelm; to make an end of; — said of flame and fire, of things burning, and figuratively of sensations and emotions; as, to quench flame; to quench a candle; to quench thirst, love, hate, etc.
q: Ere our blood shall quench that fire.
The supposition of the lady's death Will quench the wonder of her infamy.

senses.d: To cool suddenly, as heated steel, in tempering.

Quench.syn: To extinguish; still; stifle; allay; cool; check.
Quench.etym: [OE. quenchen, AS. cwencan in ācwencan, to extinguish utterly, causative of cwincan, ācwincan, to decrease, disappear; cf. AS. cwīnan, ācwīnan, to waste or dwindle away.]

senses.d: To become extinguished; to go out; to become calm or cool.
q: Dost thou think in time She will not quench!

senses.d: The act of asking; interrogation; inquiry; as, to examine by question and answer.
Discussion; debate; hence, objection; dispute; doubt; as, the story is true beyond question; he obeyed without question.
q: There arose a question between some of John's disciples and the Jews about purifying.
It is to be to question, whether it be lawful for Christian princes to make an invasive war simply for the propagation of the faith.

senses.d: Examination with reference to a decisive result; investigation; specifically, a judicial or official investigation; also, examination under torture.
q: He that was in question for the robbery. Shak. The Scottish privy council had power to put state prisoners to the question.

senses.d: That which is asked; inquiry; interrogatory; query.
q: But this question asked Puts me in doubt. Lives there who loves his pain ?

senses.d: Hence, a subject of investigation, examination, or debate; theme of inquiry; matter to be inquired into; as, a delicate or doubtful question.
Talk; conversation; speech; speech.

Question.etym: [F., fr. L. quaestio, fr. quaerere, quaesitum, to seek for, ask, inquire. See Quest, n.]

senses.d: To ask questions; to inquire.
q: He that questioneth much shall learn much.

senses.d: To argue; to converse; to dispute.
q: I pray you, think you question with the Jew.

senses.d: To inquire of by asking questions; to examine by interrogatories; as, to question a witness.
To doubt of; to be uncertain of; to query.
q: And most we question what we most desire.

senses.d: To raise a question about; to call in question; to make objection to.
To talk to; to converse with.
q: With many holiday and lady terms he questioned me.

Question.syn: To ask; interrogate; catechise; doubt; controvert; dispute.

senses.d: Alive; living; animate; — opposed to dead or inanimate.
q: Not fully quyke, ne fully dead they were.
The Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom.
Man is no star, but a quick coal Of mortal fire.

senses.d: Characterized by life or liveliness; animated; sprightly; agile; brisk; ready.
Speedy; hasty; swift; not slow; as, be quick.
q: Oft he to her his charge of quick return Repeated.

senses.d: Impatient; passionate; hasty; eager; eager; sharp; unceremonious; as, a quick temper.
q: The bishop was somewhat quick with them, and signified that he was much offended.

senses.d: Fresh; bracing; sharp; keen.
q: The air is quick there, And it pierces and sharpens the stomach.

senses.d: Sensitive; perceptive in a high degree; ready; as, a quick ear.
q: They say that women are so quick.

senses.d: Pregnant; with child.

Quick.syn: Speedy; expeditious; swift; rapid; hasty; prompt; ready; active; brisk; nimble; fleet; alert; agile; lively; sprightly.
Quick.etym: [As. cwic, cwicu, cwucu, cucu, living; akin to OS. quik, D. kwik, OHG. quec, chec, G. keck bold, lively, Icel. kvikr living, Goth. qius, Lith. qȳvas, Russ. zhivoi, L. vivus living, vivere to live, Gr. βίοσ life, Skr. jīva living, jīv to live. Cf. Biography, Vivid, Quitch grass, Whitlow.]

senses.d: In a quick manner; quickly; promptly; rapidly; with haste; speedily; without delay; as, run quick; get back quick.
q: If we consider how very quick the actions of the mind are performed.

senses.d: That which is quick, or alive; a living animal or plant; especially, the hawthorn, or other plants used in making a living hedge.
q: The works . . . are curiously hedged with quick.

senses.d: The life; the mortal point; a vital part; a part susceptible of serious injury or keen feeling; the sensitive living flesh; the part of a finger or toe to which the nail is attached; the tender emotions; as, to cut a finger nail to the quick; to thrust a sword to the quick, to taunt one to the quick; — used figuratively.
q: This test nippeth, . . . this toucheth the quick.
How feebly and unlike themselves they reason when they come to the quick of the difference !

senses.d: Quitch grass.
To revive; to quicken; to be or become alive.
To make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death or an inanimate state; hence, to excite; to, stimulate; to incite.
q: The mistress which I serve quickens what's dead.
Like a fruitful garden without an hedge, that quickens the appetite to enjoy so tempting a prize.

senses.d: To make lively, active, or sprightly; to impart additional energy to; to stimulate; to make quick or rapid; to hasten; to accelerate; as, to quicken one's steps or thoughts; to quicken one's departure or speed.
To shorten the radius of (a curve); to make (a curve) sharper; as, to quicken the sheer, that is, to make its curve more pronounced.

Quicken.syn: To revive; resuscitate; animate; reinvigorate; vivify; refresh; stimulate; sharpen; incite; hasten; accelerate; expedite; dispatch; speed.

senses.d: To come to life; to become alive; to become vivified or enlivened; hence, to exhibit signs of life; to move, as the fetus in the womb.
q: The heart is the first part that quickens, and the last that dies.
And keener lightnings quicken in her eye.
When the pale and bloodless east began To quicken to the sun.

senses.d: To move with rapidity or activity; to become accelerated; as, his pulse quickened.
The act or process of making or of becoming quick.

The first motion of the fetus in the womb felt by the mother, occurring usually about the middle of the term of pregnancy. It has been popularly supposed to be due to the fetus becoming possessed of independent life.
Speedily; with haste or celerity; soon; without delay; quick.

Sand easily moved or readily yielding to pressure; especially, a deep mass of loose or moving sand mixed with water, sometimes found at the mouth of a river or along some coasts, and very dangerous, from the difficulty of extricating a person who begins sinking into it.
q: Life hath quicksands, — Life hath snares!

senses.d: In a state of rest or calm; without stir, motion, or agitation; still; as, a quiet sea; quiet air.
q: They . . . were quiet all the night, saying, In the morning, when it is day, we shall kill him.

senses.d: Free from noise or disturbance; hushed; still.
Not excited or anxious; calm; peaceful; placid; settled; as, a quiet life; a quiet conscience.
q: That son, who on the quiet state of man Such trouble brought.

senses.d: Not giving offense; not exciting disorder or trouble; not turbulent; gentle; mild; meek; contented.
q: The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
I will sit as quiet as a lamb.

senses.d: Not showy; not such as to attract attention; undemonstrative; as, a quiet dress; quiet colors; a quiet movement.

Quiet.syn: Still; tranquil; calm; unruffled; smooth; unmolested; undisturbed; placid; peaceful; mild; peaceable; meek; contented.
Quiet.etym: [L. quietus, p. p. pf quiescere to rest, keep quiet; akin to quies rest, and prob. to E. while, n. See While, and cf. Coy, a., Quiesce, Quietus, Quit, a., Quite, Requiem.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being quiet, or in repose; as an hour or a time of quiet.
Freedom from disturbance, noise, or alarm; stillness; tranquillity; peace; security.
q: And join with thee, calm Peace and Quiet.

senses.d: To stop motion in; to still; to reduce to a state of rest, or of silence.
To calm; to appease; to pacify; to lull; to allay; to tranquillize; as, to quiet the passions; to quiet clamors or disorders; to quiet pain or grief.
q: Quiet yourselves, I pray, and be at peace.

senses.d: To become still, silent, or calm; — often with down; as, be soon quieted down.
In a quiet state or manner; without motion; in a state of rest; as, to lie or sit quietly.
Without tumult, alarm, dispute, or disturbance; peaceably; as, to live quietly; to sleep quietly.
Calmly, without agitation or violent emotion; patiently; as, to submit quietly to unavoidable evils.
Noiselessly; silently; without remark or violent movement; in a manner to attract little or no observation; as, he quietly left the room.
The quality or state of being quiet; freedom from noise, agitation, disturbance, or excitement; stillness; tranquillity; calmness.
q: I would have peace and quietness.

senses.d: Any one of numerous species of small passerine birds native of tropical America. See Banana quit, under Banana, and Guitguit.
Released from obligation, charge, penalty, etc.; free; clear; absolved; acquitted.
q: The owner of the ox shall be quit.

Quit.etym: [OE. quite, OF. quite, F. quitte. See Quit, v., Quiet.]

senses.d: To set at rest; to free, as from anything harmful or oppressive; to relieve; to clear; to liberate.
q: To quit you of this fear, you have already looked Death in the face; what have you found so terrible in it?

senses.d: To release from obligation, accusation, penalty, or the like; to absolve; to acquit.
q: There may no gold them quyte.
God will relent, and quit thee all his debt.

senses.d: To discharge, as an obligation or duty; to meet and satisfy, as a claim or debt; to make payment for or of; to requite; to repay.
q: The blissful martyr quyte you your meed.
Enkindle all the sparks of nature To quit this horrid act.
Before that judge that quits each soul his hire.

senses.d: To meet the claims upon, or expectations entertained of; to conduct; to acquit; — used reflexively.
q: Be strong, and quit yourselves like men.
Samson hath quit himself Like Samson.

senses.d: To carry through; to go through to the end.
q: Never worthy prince a day did quit With greater hazard and with more renown.

senses.d: To have done with; to cease from; to stop; hence, to depart from; to leave; to forsake; as, to quit work; to quit the place; to quit jesting.
q: Such a superficial way of examining is to quit truth for appearance.
Does not the earth quit scores with all the elements in the noble fruits that issue from it?

Quit.syn: To leave; relinquish; resign; abandon; forsake; surrender; discharge; requite.
Quit.etym: [OE. quiten, OF. quiter, quitier, cuitier, F. quitter, to acquit, quit, LL. quietare, fr. L. quietare to calm, to quiet, fr. quietus quiet. See Quiet, a., and cf. Quit, a., Quite, Acquit, Requite.]

senses.d: To go away; to depart; to stop doing a thing; to cease.
Completely; wholly; entirely; totally; perfectly; as, the work is not quite done; the object is quite accomplished; to be quite mistaken.
q: Man shall not quite be lost, but saved who will.
The same actions may be aimed at different ends, and arise from quite contrary principles.

senses.d: To a great extent or degree; very; very much; considerably.
q: He really looks quite concerned.
The island stretches along the land and is quite close to it.

Quite.etym: [F. quitte discharged, free, clear; cf. OF. quitement freely, frankly, entirely. See Quit, a.]

senses.d: Nimble; active.

Quiver.etym: [Akin to AS. cwiferlice anxiously; cf. OD. kuiven, kuiveren. Cf. Quaver.]

senses.d: To shake or move with slight and tremulous motion; to tremble; to quake; to shudder; to shiver.
q: The green leaves quiver with the cooling wind.
And left the limbs still quivering on the ground.

senses.d: The act or state of quivering; a tremor.
A case or sheath for arrows to be carried on the person.
q: Beside him hung his bow And quiver, with three-bolted thunder stored.

Quiver.etym: [OF. cuivre, cuevre, coivre, LL. cucurum, fr. OHG. chohhāri quiver, receptacle, G. köcher quiver; akin to AS. cocor, cocur, cocer, D. koker. Cf. Cocker a high shoe.]

senses.d: Furnished with, or carrying, a quiver.
Sheathed, as in a quiver.
